title: "Transforming Data"

# Transforming Data

These adaptors change items or how sequences sit next to each other. They are lazy. A `collect` or a `for` at the end runs them.

## The concept

`map` turns each item into one item. `flat_map` and `flatten` turn each item into zero or more items and splice those into one sequence. `zip` stops at the shorter side. `enumerate` pairs an index. `chain` runs a second iterator after the first is exhausted.

## Recipe 12 — Transforming every element with map()

```rust
fn main() {
    let celsius = [0, 20, 100];
    let fahrenheit: Vec<_> = celsius.iter().map(|c| c * 9 / 5 + 32).collect();
    assert_eq!(fahrenheit, [32, 68, 212]);
}
```

The closure receives `&i32` because `iter` yields references. Integer arithmetic on references works through deref. If the body needs an owned value, write `|c| { let c = *c; ... }` or use `into_iter` on a copyable array, which yields `i32` by value.

## Recipe 13 — Flattening nested collections with flat_map()

`flat_map` maps each input to something iterable, then yields those inner items one by one.

```rust
fn main() {
    let lines = ["ada,linus", "grace", ""];
    let names: Vec<&str> = lines
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|line| line.split(',').filter(|part| !part.is_empty()))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada", "linus", "grace"]);
}
```

`split` yields an iterator of `&str`. `flat_map` flattens those iterators. The empty line contributes nothing because its only split piece is empty and `filter` drops it. A `map` here would have produced a `Vec` of split iterators, not a `Vec` of names.

## Recipe 14 — Collapsing nested iterators with flatten()

`flatten` is `flat_map` with the identity function. Use it when the items are already iterators, `Option`s, or `Result`s. `Option` and `Result` implement `IntoIterator`: `Some(x)` and `Ok(x)` yield `x`, and `None` and `Err` yield nothing.

```rust
fn main() {
    let groups = vec![vec![1, 2], vec![], vec![3]];
    let flat: Vec<_> = groups.into_iter().flatten().collect();
    assert_eq!(flat, [1, 2, 3]);

    let maybe = vec![Some(4), None, Some(5)];
    let present: Vec<_> = maybe.into_iter().flatten().collect();
    assert_eq!(present, [4, 5]);
}
```

`flatten` on `Result` drops the error value. If you need to keep the first error, do not flatten. Collect into `Result<Vec<_>, _>` instead. That recipe is in the error-handling chapter.

## Recipe 15 — Pairing elements from two iterators with zip()

`zip` yields pairs until one side ends. Extra items on the longer side are not consumed only in the sense that they are never pulled. If that side is a collection you still own, those items remain in the collection. If you passed an owning iterator, the leftovers are dropped with the iterator.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
    let scores = [10, 8];
    let rows: Vec<_> = names.iter().zip(scores).collect();
    assert_eq!(rows, [(&"ada", 10), (&"linus", 8)]);
}
```

`grace` has no score, so there is no third pair. If missing partners are a bug, compare lengths before zipping, or use a form that records the mismatch instead of silently stopping.

## Recipe 16 — Attaching an index with enumerate()

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
    let numbered: Vec<_> = names.iter().enumerate().collect();
    assert_eq!(numbered, [(0, &"ada"), (1, &"linus"), (2, &"grace")]);

    let linus_at = names.iter().position(|name| *name == "linus");
    assert_eq!(linus_at, Some(1));
}
```

The index counts items this iterator has yielded, starting at 0. It is not a slice index once you have `filter`ed. After `filter`, the numbers have holes relative to the original vector. If you need the original index, `enumerate` before `filter`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = ["ada", "", "grace"];
    let kept: Vec<_> = names
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(_, name)| !name.is_empty())
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [(0, &"ada"), (2, &"grace")]);
}
```

## Recipe 17 — Concatenating iterators with chain()

```rust
fn main() {
    let morning = [1, 2];
    let evening = [8, 9];
    let day: Vec<_> = morning.into_iter().chain(evening).collect();
    assert_eq!(day, [1, 2, 8, 9]);
}
```

`chain` does not allocate. It pulls the first iterator to completion, then the second. To append one extra item, `chain(std::iter::once(0))`. To repeat a pattern, `cycle` exists, and it is infinite, so pair it with `take`.
